name: Rhodiola rosea
summary: Adaptogen for fatigue, stress and low mood; a 2012 systematic review of 11 RCTs found significant reduction in physical and mental fatigue, and an RCT (340-680mg/day) improved depression scores.
how: Standardized extract (3% rosavins, 1% salidroside) 200-600mg daily, morning on empty stomach; cycle 5 days on, 2 off.
safety: Insomnia if taken late. Interacts with antidepressants (SSRIs, MAOIs), blood pressure and diabetes drugs; amplifies caffeine. Avoid in pregnancy.
origin: Himalayan and Siberian high-altitude remedy for wind (rLung) imbalance, exhaustion and cold.

name: Cordyceps
summary: Fungal tonic for stamina and lung function; trials show improved VO2max in elderly and ~7% better exercise tolerance with CS-4 strain, plus reduced exercise lactate.
how: CS-4 cultured extract 1,000-3,000mg daily as capsules or powder; traditionally simmered in chicken or duck broth.
safety: May lower blood sugar (caution with diabetes drugs), increase bleeding risk (stop before surgery), and interact with immunosuppressants. Avoid with autoimmune disease; products are often adulterated.
origin: Noticed by Tibetan yak herders; the rGyud-bZhi says it replenishes lung essence.

name: Sea Buckthorn
summary: Berry and oil rich in omega-7 and vitamins A/D/E/K/C; an RCT of 2g/day oil reduced dry-eye symptoms, and trials show better skin hydration plus lower total cholesterol and LDL.
how: Berries as juice or jam, oil capsules 500-2000mg/day, or topical oil for skin; juice is very tart, mix with honey.
safety: May increase bleeding risk (stop 2 weeks before surgery) and lower blood pressure; interacts with blood thinners and diabetes medications. Berry allergy possible.
origin: Listed in the rGyud-bZhi for blood, lung and digestive disorders; fed to Mongol war horses.

name: Shilajit
summary: Fulvic-acid-rich mineral resin used as a rejuvenator; an RCT of purified shilajit 250mg twice daily for 90 days raised total testosterone ~20% in healthy men, with antioxidant and mitochondrial effects.
how: Purified resin, pea-sized (~300-500mg) dissolved in warm water or milk once or twice daily.
safety: Use ONLY purified forms; raw material may carry heavy metals and mycotoxins. May lower blood pressure and boost iron absorption (avoid in hemochromatosis); interacts with diabetes and blood pressure drugs. Not in pregnancy.
origin: Rock essence of the Himalaya, a rasayana in both Tibetan and Ayurvedic medicine.

name: Terminalia chebula
summary: The King of Medicines in Sowa Rigpa; chebulagic acid inhibits alpha-glucosidase like acarbose, animal studies show lower fasting glucose, and it acts as a gentle motility-stimulating laxative and broad antimicrobial.
how: 1-3g powder in warm water before bed; or as Triphala; decoction as mouthwash; topical paste for wounds.
safety: Diarrhea at high doses. Avoid in pregnancy (may stimulate uterine contractions). Enhances diabetes and blood pressure medications; may increase bleeding risk.
origin: Held in the hand of the Medicine Buddha and used in over half of classical Tibetan formulas.

name: Camphor
summary: Topical analgesic and decongestant, FDA-approved at 3-11%; it activates TRPV1/TRPA1 to block pain signals, and a Pediatrics RCT found camphor vapor rub improved children's night cough and congestion.
how: TOPICAL ONLY: creams or ointments 3-11%, or steam inhalation. Apply diluted to chest and cover.
safety: TOXIC IF SWALLOWED - as little as 2g can kill an adult; can cause seizures. Never on broken skin, never near infants' nostrils (respiratory collapse). Not for internal use.
origin: Used in Tibetan precious pills, chest rubs and purifying incense.

name: Long Pepper
summary: Classic bioavailability enhancer: its piperine raises curcumin absorption by up to 2000% and boosts many herbs and drugs; piperlongumine shows bronchodilatory effects supporting traditional cough use.
how: 250-500mg powder with honey or in food; classic Trikatu blend with ginger and black pepper; whole pods in cooking.
safety: Raises absorption of medications - dangerous with narrow-therapeutic-index drugs (digoxin, phenytoin). Increases gastric acid; avoid with ulcers. Caution in pregnancy.
origin: Sowa Rigpa used it to make other herbs work better, and for cold/phlegm and weak digestion.

name: Tibetan Precious Pills
summary: Complex multi-herb formulas for chronic disease; evidence is preliminary except Padma 28, which has 100+ studies of anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects and is a registered pharmaceutical in Switzerland. A pilot study suggested post-stroke functional gains.
how: Only under a trained Tibetan physician; authentic pills come from Men-Tsee-Khang institutes. Not for self-prescription.
safety: Some contain processed metals (mercury, gold) of debated safety. Not standardized; quality and authenticity vary. Avoid in pregnancy.
origin: The most revered Sowa Rigpa preparations, made by ritual over days or weeks.

name: Fermented Mare's Milk
summary: Probiotic ferment (10^7-10^8 CFU/mL of Lactobacillus and yeasts) with 400x the lysozyme of cow's milk; 19th-century kumiss cures documented improvement in TB patients, and observational studies link it to lower cholesterol and blood pressure.
how: 1-2 cups fresh airag daily where available; freeze-dried mare's milk products exist; kefir is a close substitute.
safety: Contains alcohol (0.7-2.5%, up to 6%). Still contains some lactose - may affect severely lactose-intolerant people. Hard to source outside Central Asia.
origin: Fermented in leather khokhuur by nomads for millennia; carried as field medicine by Genghis Khan's armies.

name: Mongolian Astragalus
summary: Immune tonic whose astragalosides activate T-cells and NK cells; a 2019 meta-analysis found astragalus injection improved cardiac output in chronic heart failure alongside standard care, and reviews show reduced proteinuria in diabetic nephropathy.
how: Dried root slices simmered 15-20 min in soup, broth or tea, or standardized extract 500-2000mg daily.
safety: Interacts with immunosuppressants (avoid post-transplant) and blood thinners; may lower blood sugar. Avoid with autoimmune disease and during acute infections.
origin: Long used by Mongolian herders for weakness and recovery from illness.

name: Ephedra
summary: Source of ephedrine and pseudoephedrine, potent bronchodilators and decongestants; the pharmaceutical derivatives are well proven, but a JAMA meta-analysis found herbal ephedra gave only modest weight loss with serious cardiovascular risk.
how: NOT recommended for self-use. Herbal supplements were banned by the FDA in 2004; use OTC pseudoephedrine for congestion instead.
safety: DANGEROUS: heart attack, stroke, seizures and deaths reported. Raises blood pressure and heart rate. Interacts with MAOIs, blood pressure drugs, stimulants and caffeine. Never with heart conditions.
origin: Used on the Mongolian steppe and in Chinese medicine for breathing difficulty, colds and fever.

name: Sea Buckthorn (Mongolian use)
summary: Same berry as the Tibetan star-bu, used in Mongolia as a winter vitamin C source and skin protectant; the clinical evidence for skin, dry eye and cholesterol applies equally here.
how: Oil applied for winter skin protection, berries or juice for vitamin C, leaf tea for digestion; juice mixed with airag is a traditional drink.
safety: As for sea buckthorn generally: bleeding risk (stop 2 weeks before surgery), may lower blood pressure, interacts with blood thinners and diabetes drugs.
origin: Mongolia's vast wild sea buckthorn forests make it one of the world's largest producers.

name: Andrographis
aka: fah talai jone, king of bitters, kalmegh
summary: Leading cold and flu herb: a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (n=807) found andrographolides significantly improved cold symptoms versus placebo, and the Kan Jang combination reduced cold severity and duration.
how: Standardized extract (10-30% andrographolides) 200-400mg, 2-3x daily at the first sign of a cold; take with food.
safety: Nausea, diarrhea, headache. Anti-platelet effect - caution with blood thinners; may lower blood pressure; interacts with immunosuppressants. May affect fertility at high doses. Avoid in pregnancy.
origin: The primary Thai remedy for fever and infection, also Ayurveda's kalmegh.

name: Mangosteen
summary: The rind holds 60+ xanthones; alpha-mangostin inhibits COX-2, iNOS and NF-kB in lab studies and is active against MRSA and H. pylori. Cell studies suggest possible complementary support only - no human cancer trials exist.
how: Eat the fresh flesh; pericarp extract capsules 500-1500mg daily or dried pericarp tea. Most juices contain few xanthones.
safety: Pericarp extracts may slow clotting - avoid before surgery and with blood thinners. Rare lactic acidosis at very high doses. May interact with chemotherapy drugs; juices often have added sugar.
origin: Rind used for centuries in Thai, Malay and Indonesian medicine for dysentery and skin infections.

name: Tongkat Ali
summary: Male tonic: an RCT of 200mg/day for 4 weeks raised testosterone and lowered cortisol, tension and anger in stressed adults, and a 9-month study improved sperm concentration and motility.
how: Standardized root extract 200-400mg daily (1-2% eurycomanone), taken in the morning; cycle 5 days on, 2 off.
safety: May raise heart rate and cause insomnia or restlessness. Interacts with diabetes and blood pressure medications; caution with hormone-sensitive conditions. Not for children or pregnant/nursing women; adulteration is common.
origin: Ali's walking stick - a bitter root decoction used as an aphrodisiac across Malaysia and Indonesia.

name: Centella asiatica
aka: gotu kola, bai bua bok, pegaga
summary: Triterpenes (asiaticoside, madecassoside) stimulate collagen and angiogenesis; clinical trials confirm faster wound healing, an RCT showed significant improvement in chronic venous insufficiency, and 750mg/day improved memory and mood in elderly subjects.
how: Fresh leaves in salads or juice; standardized TTFCA extract 60-120mg daily for venous problems; topical cream for scars; leaf tea.
safety: Nausea, headache, drowsiness; rare hepatotoxicity at high doses - monitor liver function long-term. Increases sun sensitivity. Interacts with sedatives, diabetes drugs and cholesterol medications. Avoid in pregnancy.
origin: A longevity and wound herb shared by Southeast Asian medicine, Ayurveda and TCM.

name: Galangal
summary: Culinary rhizome whose 1'-acetoxychavicol acetate is a potent NF-kB inhibitor; it is active against H. pylori, resistant bacteria and Candida, protects gastric mucosa and eases nausea much like ginger.
how: Fresh root in soups and curries (Tom Kha Gai), sliced as tea, 1-3g dried powder in capsules, or chew fresh slices for nausea.
safety: Very safe in food amounts. High doses may irritate the GI tract; raw slices can irritate mouth and throat. May interact with blood thinners.
origin: A cornerstone of Thai food-as-medicine and Indonesian jamu.

name: Lemongrass
summary: Citral gives broad antibacterial and antifungal activity including against Candida; it inhibits HMG-CoA reductase (weak statin-like effect) and the essential oil showed GABAergic anxiolytic effects in animals.
how: Fresh stalks in soups and curries; tea steeped 5-10 min; diluted essential oil topically for muscle pain; aromatherapy.
safety: Do not ingest the essential oil, and avoid it in pregnancy. Can cause contact dermatitis. May lower blood sugar and interact with sedatives.
origin: The fever grass of Thai, Vietnamese, Indonesian and Filipino kitchens and medicine chests.

name: Pandan
aka: Pandanus amaryllifolius, vanilla of the East
summary: Aromatic leaf with hypoglycemic effects demonstrated in diabetic animal models plus mild sedative and antioxidant activity; human clinical data are still lacking.
how: Fresh leaves knotted into cooking rice, curries and desserts; pandan juice (blended leaves, strained) for drinks; leaf tea.
safety: Very safe as food. Insufficient data for therapeutic doses in pregnancy. May lower blood sugar - monitor if diabetic.
origin: Roots used for sugar disease in Thai and Malaysian folk medicine; leaves for fever and restlessness.

name: Moringa
summary: Extremely nutrient-dense leaf; pooled animal and human data show significant reductions in fasting blood glucose (about 26% in human studies) plus lower total cholesterol and LDL, and Philippine studies confirm increased breast milk production.
how: Fresh leaves in soups and stir-fries, 1-2 tsp dried leaf powder daily, or capsules 500-2000mg; seeds roasted; Ben oil for skin.
safety: Avoid root and bark internally (spirochin toxicity) and in pregnancy (possible abortifacient). Interacts with thyroid, diabetes and blood pressure medications; may lower blood pressure. Seeds can cause diarrhea.
origin: The Philippines' most-used medicinal plant, the miracle tree of the tropics.

name: Banaba Leaf
summary: Corosolic acid acts as an insulin mimetic activating GLUT4; an RCT found 10mg corosolic acid lowered blood glucose about 30% in type 2 diabetics within 2 weeks, with supporting weight and BMI reductions.
how: Leaf tea (dried leaves steeped 15 min) or extract standardized to 1% corosolic acid, 32-48mg daily; traditionally boil 10-15 fresh leaves in 2 cups water 15 min.
safety: Can cause hypoglycemia with diabetes medications - monitor blood sugar closely. Not a replacement for prescribed treatment. Limited long-term data; avoid in pregnancy.
origin: Brewed as a tea for sugar disease in Filipino folk medicine.

name: Temulawak
summary: Liver and digestive herb approved by German Commission E for liver and gallbladder complaints; xanthorrhizol is hepatoprotective, raises bile output 50-100% and inhibits COX-2, H. pylori, Candida and MRSA.
how: Traditional jamu of grated fresh rhizome boiled with tamarind and palm sugar; extract standardized to 15-30mg xanthorrhizol daily, or 2-4g powder.
safety: Avoid with gallstones or bile duct obstruction (increases bile). Interacts with liver-metabolized (CYP) medications and blood thinners. Avoid in pregnancy - may stimulate uterine contractions.
origin: The cornerstone of Javanese jamu for over 1,300 years, in nearly every jamu galian blend.

name: Kratom
summary: Informational only. Mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine are partial mu-opioid agonists; case series document analgesia and observational data suggest reduced opioid withdrawal, but no RCTs exist and risks are substantial.
how: NOT recommended for self-medication. If used at all, only low doses of verified single-ingredient product under medical supervision.
safety: SIGNIFICANT RISK: addiction, withdrawal, rare liver toxicity, respiratory depression at high dose, contaminated products, deaths in combination use. NEVER with opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol or CNS depressants. Avoid in pregnancy. Legality varies - check local law.
origin: Leaves chewed by Southeast Asian laborers for energy and pain for centuries.

name: Butterfly Pea Flower
summary: Anthocyanin-rich blue flower with antioxidant capacity rivalling blueberries; rat studies show improved memory and acetylcholinesterase inhibition, and it inhibits alpha-glucosidase to blunt glucose absorption. Human data are limited.
how: Steep 5-10 dried flowers per cup for 5-10 min; add lemon for the colour change and vitamin C. Also used in rice, desserts and as a hair rinse.
safety: Generally very safe. Mild anti-platelet effect - caution with blood thinners; may lower blood sugar; nausea in large amounts. Avoid in pregnancy/nursing as a precaution.
origin: Thai dok anchan tea and Ayurvedic brain tonic shankhpushpi.

name: Jamu Tradition
summary: Indonesia's 1,300-year-old herbal system of thousands of fresh-made formulas drawing on the country's vast plant biodiversity; individual components (turmeric, temulawak, kencur, tamarind) carry the supporting evidence.
how: Traditionally sold fresh daily by jamu gendong women; preparations are drunk fresh, often as sweet-sour herbal tonics.
safety: Unstandardized; some commercial jamu has been found adulterated with pharmaceuticals such as NSAIDs or steroids. Component-specific cautions apply (see temulawak, turmeric).
origin: A living Javanese household medicine tradition, now also produced commercially.

name: Kunyit Asam
summary: The best-studied jamu drink, made of fresh turmeric and tamarind, used for menstrual pain and skin; benefits track curcumin's anti-inflammatory action plus tamarind antioxidants.
how: Fresh turmeric and tamarind boiled with palm sugar, drunk as a daily tonic, especially around menstruation.
safety: Turmeric cautions apply: avoid high doses with gallstones, anticoagulants or before surgery, and avoid therapeutic doses in pregnancy. Contains added sugar.
origin: The most popular jamu gendong preparation in Java.

name: Beras Kencur
summary: Rice, kencur (Kaempferia galanga), tamarind and palm sugar drink for fatigue, cough and body aches; kencur's ethyl-p-methoxycinnamate has documented anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects.
how: Drunk fresh as a sweet tonic, traditionally in the morning or after physical labour.
safety: Little clinical safety data. Contains significant sugar. Avoid therapeutic amounts in pregnancy; caution alongside anti-inflammatory drugs.
origin: A children's and workers' tonic in Javanese jamu.

name: Jamu Galian Singset
summary: Multi-herb blend (temulawak, kencur, turmeric and others) taken for weight management and vitality; the combination lacks clinical trials though individual herbs have supporting data.
how: Drunk as a fresh herbal preparation, traditionally daily by women.
safety: Commercial slimming jamu has been found adulterated with pharmaceutical stimulants or laxatives - buy carefully. Temulawak/turmeric cautions apply: gallstones, anticoagulants, pregnancy.
origin: A classic women's tonic in the Javanese jamu repertoire.

name: Thai Massage
summary: Clothed floor-based bodywork combining acupressure and passive stretching; an RCT found it as effective as joint mobilization for chronic low back pain, and trials show reduced tension headache and salivary cortisol.
how: Sessions of 1-2 hours on a floor mat, fully clothed; weekly for chronic conditions.
safety: Not for acute injuries, fractures, deep vein thrombosis, fever, osteoporosis, recent surgery or skin infections. Overly aggressive technique can injure - state your pain tolerance clearly.
origin: A 2,500-year-old system attributed to the Buddha's physician; UNESCO heritage listed in 2019.

name: Tibetan Singing Bowl Therapy
summary: Sound meditation using metal bowls; a 2017 study found significant reductions in tension, anxiety, depression and anger plus lower systolic and diastolic blood pressure, though samples were small and unblinded.
how: Sessions with a trained practitioner (bowls on or near the body), or self-practice with a personal bowl during meditation.
safety: Vibration may overwhelm trauma survivors. Not recommended near pacemakers or implanted electrical devices. Not a substitute for mental health treatment.
origin: Metal bowls used in Tibetan Buddhist practice to support meditative states.
